transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess the main thing is this memorial I’ve been trying to put together for my brother. It started off as something simple, you know, just a way to honor him, maybe have some music and a few pictures, but it’s gotten much bigger than I meant for it to. I keep finding more things that need doing—songs he liked, people I should call, displays I could make, places tied to him I ought to visit or include somehow—and before I know it, whole days are gone.

My wife says I’ve been spending most of my time chasing all of that down, calling folks, planning little trips, arranging things in my head and on paper, and she says I’ve pushed aside everything else. The garden’s been sitting there, I haven’t been going with my walking group like I usually do, and honestly a lot of the regular day-to-day stuff has just kind of fallen away. So… that’s what brings me in, I suppose. It’s gotten hard to slow it down.
Do unwanted thoughts about the memorial keep popping into your mind even when you try not to think about it?

I’m not sure I’d call them “unwanted thoughts,” exactly. It’s more like once I start thinking about the memorial, one thing leads to another and then I’m off in it again. Like I’ll see something in the house, or remember a song, or think of someone who knew my brother, and then I start wondering whether that should be part of it somehow.

I can’t say I’ve really sat there trying not to think about it and had it force its way in, if that’s what you mean. It’s more… it just keeps taking up space because there’s always another detail, another idea. Sometimes I don’t even realize I’ve gone back to it until I’ve spent an hour making notes or looking something up. So, I don’t know. It keeps coming up, yes, but I’m not sure it feels like an intrusive thing in the way you’re asking.
Have you been feeling unusually cheerful or euphoric lately?

Yeah… cheerful maybe isn’t exactly the word I’d use, but there are times lately where I feel, I don’t know, lit up. Like everything about this memorial suddenly feels so clear and important, like I’ve got this purpose and if I can just get it right, then people in town are finally going to understand my brother, and understand our family, and what all of it meant.

And when I’m in that feeling, it can feel almost good—more than good, really, like I’m carrying something that matters. But it doesn’t stay soft or pleasant. If my wife asks me to slow down, or says maybe the display doesn’t need another section, I can snap at her. Same with people at the senior center, if they question how I’m setting things up or they don’t move fast enough. I get irritated quick, like they’re getting in the way of something important.

So… yes, there’s been this high feeling, but it’s mixed with me getting sharp with people too.
Lately, have you been needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling full of energy?

I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. I mean, my sleep has been a bit all over the place, but I haven’t been keeping track of it the way maybe I should. Some nights I’m up later than I meant to be because I get caught up thinking through details or writing something down, and then I look at the clock and it’s later than I expected.

But whether I’m needing much less sleep and still feeling full of energy… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to say that exactly if I don’t know. There are times I keep going when my wife thinks I should stop, and I’ll tell her I’m fine, I’ve got things to finish, but I also don’t know how much of that is energy and how much is just me not wanting to leave things undone.

So… maybe I’ve been staying up more, but I haven’t really noticed it as “I don’t need sleep anymore” or anything like that. It’s hard for me to separate.
Have you been feeling more important or specially capable than usual lately?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. “More important” sounds a little… big, like I’m walking around thinking I’m better than people, and I don’t think that’s what I feel. At least I don’t notice myself thinking that.

I do feel like what I’m doing matters, maybe more than other people seem to understand, and sometimes that makes me feel like I’m the one who has to make sure it comes out right. But specially capable? I don’t know. I’ve always been particular about things when they matter to me. My wife might say I’m acting like I’m the only one who can handle it, but from inside it just feels like I’m trying to do it properly.

So… I guess I haven’t really noticed feeling powerful or superior or anything like that. More like I feel responsible, and maybe I’m holding on to it too tightly.
Have you done anything lately that felt out of character or risky for you?

Risky? I don’t know… I guess I’m not sure what counts as risky in the way you mean.

I haven’t, like, gone out and done something wild on purpose, if that’s what you’re asking. I’m not thinking of anything where I’d say, “That was completely unlike me and dangerous.” Mostly I’ve just been wrapped up in getting things right, and maybe I’ve pushed harder than people around me would like. But when I’m doing it, it doesn’t feel risky exactly—it feels necessary, or like I’m trying to finish what I started.

Out of character… maybe my wife would have a better answer, honestly. She might say I’ve been more intense or stubborn than usual. But from my side, I can’t point to some big thing, like spending a bunch of money or taking off somewhere or doing something reckless. I don’t think so. Nothing like that comes to mind.
Have you started to believe things about the memorial or your brother that other people say aren’t true or seem unrealistic?

Well… yes, I suppose that’s closer to what my wife has been worried about. I know how it’s going to sound when I say it out loud, and I’m not trying to make it sound dramatic, but there are these old ballads my brother kept—songs he cared about—and I’ve been going over them because of the memorial. And the more I listen, or read the words, the more I’m sure there are warnings in them.

Not just memories, not just “oh, this reminds me of him.” I mean warnings meant for me. Certain lines stand out in a way they didn’t before, like he left something there, or like I’m supposed to understand what to do from them. My wife says I’m reading too much into it, that they’re just songs and grief makes people connect things. I understand why she’d say that. But I know what I heard in those words. It isn’t random to me.

And I know you might say that sounds unrealistic, but it feels very clear when I’m with them. Like there’s a message tucked underneath the plain meaning, and if I ignore it, I’d be missing something important from my brother.
Did all of this start after your brother died?

Yes… yes, it really did. I mean, not the very minute he died, if you know what I mean, but it all began after that. It’s been about two months now, since he passed, and especially since I started working on the tribute for him.

At first it just felt like normal grieving, trying to pull things together and make the memorial mean something. I was going through things connected to him, thinking about what would honor him properly, and then it sort of… grew from there. The songs, the meaning of them, the feeling that I needed to get it right—that all started in that period after his death.

So yes, I’d say it’s been going on for around two months, tied pretty directly to losing him and planning the memorial.
Have you been talking more than usual lately?

Yes… I think so. I don’t always notice it while it’s happening, but people have pointed it out.

Like at the senior center meetings, if we start talking about the memorial, I’ll begin explaining the songs, and then that leads into the quilts, and then the photos, and how each one fits with my brother, and before I know it I’ve gone on and on. I’m not trying to take over, but I’ll realize I’ve talked right over two or three people who were trying to add something.

My pastor has had to sort of gently step in and say, “Aaron, let’s let someone else speak,” which is embarrassing when I think about it afterward. At the time, though, it feels like I need to get the whole thought out before it disappears or before someone misunderstands what I mean. So yes, I suppose I have been talking more than usual.
Have you been more active than usual lately, always starting projects or feeling driven to keep doing things?

Yes, I have. That’s actually something my wife keeps bringing up too, because I used to be able to sit in my chair for a while, you know, have my coffee, read the paper, maybe doze off a little in the afternoon. Lately I can’t seem to do that. I’ll sit down and then two minutes later I’m back up again because I remembered a box that needs sorting or a phone call I ought to make, or I’ll think the papers for the memorial aren’t in the right order and I need to rearrange them.

I’ve been hauling boxes around the house, moving things from one room to another, spreading photographs and notes out on the table, then deciding they belong somewhere else. I’ll walk from the living room to the kitchen and back again, then down the hall, then back to the table, like I’m following some thread I can’t quite hold onto unless I keep moving.

It feels like my body has more steam in it than a man my age ought to have. I’m sixty-nine, I know I shouldn’t be running myself like this, but when I try to stop, it feels wrong, like there’s still something unfinished pressing on me. So yes, more active than usual, definitely.
Have these changes caused serious problems in your daily life or relationships?

Yes… yes, it has. I don’t like saying that, because in my mind I keep telling myself this is for my brother, so it’s important, and people should understand that. But if I’m honest, it’s gotten in the way of ordinary life.

I’ve missed my walking group several times, and I used to be pretty regular with that. Same with book club — I just don’t go, or I tell myself I’ll go after I finish one more thing for the memorial display, and then the time passes. The garden’s been neglected too. My wife pointed that out to me because I’ve always kept up with it, even if it was just a little trimming or watering, and now it’s just sitting there because all my attention goes to these photos and notes and arrangements.

And at the senior center… I think I’ve upset some people. I don’t mean to, but every conversation somehow turns into the memorial. Someone will mention something completely different, and I’ll bring it back to my brother or the display or what song should be played, and I can see people get tired or uncomfortable. A couple friends have pulled back, I think.

My wife says our whole day has become about either calming me down or trying to redirect me — stopping me from making another phone call, or taking another trip over to the center, or getting into another argument about how things should be set up. She says it’s like there’s no normal day anymore, just managing whatever I’m focused on next. That hurt to hear, but… I suppose she’s not wrong.
Have you heard your brother speaking to you when no one else was there?

Yes… I have. I almost don’t like saying it out loud because it sounds strange, but yes.

It happens mostly when I’m at the kitchen table with his song sheets spread out in front of me. I’ll be sorting through them, trying to put them in the right order, and I’ll hear him — my brother — clear as day. Sometimes it’s like he’s behind me humming one of the tunes, just soft, like he used to do when he was thinking. Other times it’s more like he’s telling me which song comes next, like, “No, Aaron, that one goes after this one,” and I’ll turn or pause because it feels so real.

But nobody else hears it. My wife will be in the house and I’ll ask, “Did you hear that?” or I’ll look up like someone just spoke, and she’ll say she didn’t hear anything. And I know he’s gone, I know that, but in the moment it doesn’t feel like a memory exactly. It feels like him, right there, helping me with the music.
Before your brother died, was there ever another time in your life when you had a similar spell of feeling unusually energized or driven, talking more than usual, or having experiences like this?

No… not like this. I mean, I’ve had busy times in my life, of course. Raising a family, working, getting through different troubles, you have periods where you’re running around and there’s a lot to do. But before my brother died, I don’t remember ever having this kind of… spell, I guess, where I felt pushed along like this, like I couldn’t leave things alone.

And the voice part — no. I never heard him in the house before. I never sat at the kitchen table and heard him humming behind me or telling me what order the songs should go in. That all started after he passed, when I got so wrapped up in the memorial work.

Same with the songs feeling like they were aimed at me somehow, like they were warning me or telling me something personal. Before all this, songs were just songs. They might make me sad or remind me of something, sure, but they weren’t sending me messages. That feeling came along with this whole burst of energy and the planning and rearranging and not being able to stop. So no, I can’t say there was another time like this before.
Before this time, had you ever had a period in your life when you felt unusually high, energized, or driven like this?

Before this? No, not really in the same way. I mean, I’ve had days where I was in a good mood or busy with something, but not this feeling of being… lit up, I guess. Full of purpose. Like I suddenly know exactly what has to be done and everybody else just needs to understand it.

With this memorial, one minute I feel almost lifted by it, like the whole town is finally going to see who my brother was and what our family meant, and it feels important in a way I can’t quite explain. But then if my wife says, “Maybe leave that alone for tonight,” or someone at the senior center questions where I put something, I can snap. I don’t like admitting that. I hear my voice get sharp, and I’ll think, why are they slowing me down, don’t they see this matters?

So before now, I don’t remember having that sort of high, driven feeling mixed with getting irritated so quickly. This has been different.

target_item.name: Pressured_Speech
target_item.manifestation: At the senior center meetings I start explaining the songs and the quilts and the photos, and before I know it I’ve talked over three people and my pastor is gently saying, ‘Aaron, let’s let someone else speak.’
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether I have been talking more than usual, which directly matches pressured speech.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I don’t always notice it while it’s happening, but people have pointed it out.

Like at the senior center meetings, if we start talking about the memorial, I’ll begin explaining the songs, and then that leads into the quilts, and then the photos, and how each one fits with my brother, and before I know it I’ve gone on and on. I’m not trying to take over, but I’ll realize I’ve talked right over two or three people who were trying to add something.

My pastor has had to sort of gently step in and say, “Aaron, let’s let someone else speak,” which is embarrassing when I think about it afterward. At the time, though, it feels like I need to get the whole thought out before it disappears or before someone misunderstands what I mean. So yes, I suppose I have been talking more than usual.

doctor.intent: Determine whether he has increased goal-directed activity, which would help distinguish a manic/hypomanic episode from a grief-related adjustment reaction.
doctor.question: Have you been more active than usual lately, always starting projects or feeling driven to keep doing things?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I can’t seem to sit in my chair like I used to; I’m up hauling boxes, making calls, rearranging papers, walking room to room, feeling like my body has more steam in it than a man my age ought to have.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about being more active than usual and feeling driven to keep doing things, which most directly matches increased activity and energy.

patient.answer:
Yes, I have. That’s actually something my wife keeps bringing up too, because I used to be able to sit in my chair for a while, you know, have my coffee, read the paper, maybe doze off a little in the afternoon. Lately I can’t seem to do that. I’ll sit down and then two minutes later I’m back up again because I remembered a box that needs sorting or a phone call I ought to make, or I’ll think the papers for the memorial aren’t in the right order and I need to rearrange them.

I’ve been hauling boxes around the house, moving things from one room to another, spreading photographs and notes out on the table, then deciding they belong somewhere else. I’ll walk from the living room to the kitchen and back again, then down the hall, then back to the table, like I’m following some thread I can’t quite hold onto unless I keep moving.

It feels like my body has more steam in it than a man my age ought to have. I’m sixty-nine, I know I shouldn’t be running myself like this, but when I try to stop, it feels wrong, like there’s still something unfinished pressing on me. So yes, more active than usual, definitely.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms have caused marked impairment in functioning, which would distinguish a manic episode (bipolar I) from hypomania/adjustment-related conditions.
doctor.question: Have these changes caused serious problems in your daily life or relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve missed my walking group and book club, let the garden go, and upset friends at the senior center because everything has become about the memorial display. My wife says our days revolve around calming me down or redirecting me from another call, trip, or argument.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the mood and activity changes have caused serious problems in daily functioning or relationships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, it has. I don’t like saying that, because in my mind I keep telling myself this is for my brother, so it’s important, and people should understand that. But if I’m honest, it’s gotten in the way of ordinary life.

I’ve missed my walking group several times, and I used to be pretty regular with that. Same with book club — I just don’t go, or I tell myself I’ll go after I finish one more thing for the memorial display, and then the time passes. The garden’s been neglected too. My wife pointed that out to me because I’ve always kept up with it, even if it was just a little trimming or watering, and now it’s just sitting there because all my attention goes to these photos and notes and arrangements.

And at the senior center… I think I’ve upset some people. I don’t mean to, but every conversation somehow turns into the memorial. Someone will mention something completely different, and I’ll bring it back to my brother or the display or what song should be played, and I can see people get tired or uncomfortable. A couple friends have pulled back, I think.

My wife says our whole day has become about either calming me down or trying to redirect me — stopping me from making another phone call, or taking another trip over to the center, or getting into another argument about how things should be set up. She says it’s like there’s no normal day anymore, just managing whatever I’m focused on next. That hurt to hear, but… I suppose she’s not wrong.

inference.note: This turn strengthens a manic-spectrum episode: increased talkativeness, increased goal-directed activity/psychomotor activation, decreased functioning, irritability/elevated mood, and psychotic-like ideas centered on messages in songs. Adjustment disorder/grief reactions are less likely given syndromal manic features with possible psychotic symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the episode includes psychotic symptoms, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder, current manic episode, from hypomania.
doctor.question: Have you heard your brother speaking to you when no one else was there?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I’m sorting his song sheets at the kitchen table, I hear my brother’s voice clear as day humming behind me or telling me which tune comes next, even though nobody else in the house hears a thing.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hearing the brother speak when no one else was present, which directly concerns auditory hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Yes… I have. I almost don’t like saying it out loud because it sounds strange, but yes.

It happens mostly when I’m at the kitchen table with his song sheets spread out in front of me. I’ll be sorting through them, trying to put them in the right order, and I’ll hear him — my brother — clear as day. Sometimes it’s like he’s behind me humming one of the tunes, just soft, like he used to do when he was thinking. Other times it’s more like he’s telling me which song comes next, like, “No, Aaron, that one goes after this one,” and I’ll turn or pause because it feels so real.

But nobody else hears it. My wife will be in the house and I’ll ask, “Did you hear that?” or I’ll look up like someone just spoke, and she’ll say she didn’t hear anything. And I know he’s gone, I know that, but in the moment it doesn’t feel like a memory exactly. It feels like him, right there, helping me with the music.

inference.note: Psychotic features are now evident (auditory hallucinations, delusional interpretation of songs) along with elevated/irritable mood, increased talkativeness, increased activity, and functional impairment. This shifts the differential from hypomania/mania without psychosis to mania with psychotic symptoms; bipolar manic episode remains if prior depression is unknown.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a past manic episode, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder, current manic episode with psychotic features (F31.2), from a single manic episode with psychotic features (F30.2).
doctor.question: Before your brother died, was there ever another time in your life when you had a similar spell of feeling unusually energized or driven, talking more than usual, or having experiences like this?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Before I got swept up in this memorial work after my brother died, I never heard his voice in the house or felt the songs were sending me personal warnings; those things started along with this burst of energy and nonstop planning.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether similar manic-energy symptoms or psychotic-like experiences occurred before the current episode after the brother's death, which directly relates to whether the delusions and hallucinations only occurred during this manic episode.

patient.answer:
No… not like this. I mean, I’ve had busy times in my life, of course. Raising a family, working, getting through different troubles, you have periods where you’re running around and there’s a lot to do. But before my brother died, I don’t remember ever having this kind of… spell, I guess, where I felt pushed along like this, like I couldn’t leave things alone.

And the voice part — no. I never heard him in the house before. I never sat at the kitchen table and heard him humming behind me or telling me what order the songs should go in. That all started after he passed, when I got so wrapped up in the memorial work.

Same with the songs feeling like they were aimed at me somehow, like they were warning me or telling me something personal. Before all this, songs were just songs. They might make me sad or remind me of something, sure, but they weren’t sending me messages. That feeling came along with this whole burst of energy and the planning and rearranging and not being able to stop. So no, I can’t say there was another time like this before.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a prior manic episode, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder (current manic episode with psychotic symptoms) from a single manic episode with psychotic symptoms.
doctor.question: Before this time, had you ever had a period in your life when you felt unusually high, energized, or driven like this?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I’ll feel lit up and full of purpose one minute, like the whole town is finally going to understand our family, and then I snap at my wife or someone at the senior center if they slow me down or question the display.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether there had ever been a prior period of unusually high, energized, or driven mood, which most directly relates to elevated or expansive mood episodes.

patient.answer:
Before this? No, not really in the same way. I mean, I’ve had days where I was in a good mood or busy with something, but not this feeling of being… lit up, I guess. Full of purpose. Like I suddenly know exactly what has to be done and everybody else just needs to understand it.

With this memorial, one minute I feel almost lifted by it, like the whole town is finally going to see who my brother was and what our family meant, and it feels important in a way I can’t quite explain. But then if my wife says, “Maybe leave that alone for tonight,” or someone at the senior center questions where I put something, I can snap. I don’t like admitting that. I hear my voice get sharp, and I’ll think, why are they slowing me down, don’t they see this matters?

So before now, I don’t remember having that sort of high, driven feeling mixed with getting irritated so quickly. This has been different.

inference.note: No prior episodes of mania/hypomania were reported, making bipolar disorder with psychotic symptoms less likely. Current episode shows manic syndrome with psychotic features (elevated/irritable mood, increased activity, pressured/talkative behavior, functional impairment, delusions/auditory hallucinations) lasting about 2 months.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a first lifetime episode of elevated/irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity, pressured/overinclusive speech, and clear psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and delusional/message-like interpretations) causing marked functional impairment over about two months. There is no prior history of similar episodes, so the presentation is most consistent with a manic episode with psychotic symptoms rather than bipolar disorder. Although symptoms followed bereavement, the syndrome extends beyond normal grief and includes sustained mania with psychosis.
